posts.body:
UNTOLD 2
​
Spoiler
Work on Untold 2 technically began over 10 years ago, with consistent effort on advancing the project beginning ~6 years ago, and a desire/goal to actually publish materializing in 2024. The game is near-complete, with the goal of being released as a beta (at the very least) this December (2025). Over the past 6 months the developer has been working with a professional writer, hired to re-write dialogue, expand the narrative, and flesh-out broader world lore. Custom art is now one of the few remaining missing pieces needed to facilitate any release.
DISCLAIMERS - RELIGIOUS AND POLITICAL
Spoiler
Untold 2 contains NPCs who worship a powerful magical entity, Esmerelda, as a god. The quantity and zealousness of the faithful varies throughout the world, with towns constructed in areas where Esmerelda is more commonly sighted having significantly more.
There is a party member class called "Hospitaller" (which serves effectively as a classic Paladin). Beyond the name, the only similarity to the Christian military order is that their job lore-wise is to protect/aid injured or otherwise vulnerable people.
There are some foes the player party can fight named after angels and demons referenced in the Abrahamic religions (e.g. Azrael, Moloch, Andrammelech). There are no other pieces of Abrahamic religions referenced/incorporated beyond the names.
There are multiple states/sovereignties in the main world (Prima). The Velfarr Kingdom is a kingdom (obviously) ruled by a Royal Family with authority passed down over time through the family line. There is a political institution within Velfarr known as the Wizard Chiefs (composed of 5 wizards, any vacancy among them is filled by another wizard selected by the 4 current Chiefs). The Chiefs exist broadly to give wizards within Velfarr self-governing political autonomy. However a lax and disinterested Royal Family leaves most of the overall governing duties (and thus power) in the hands of the Wizard Chiefs, as well. Something that some non-wizard NPCs resent, as does the Grayscoh Republic.
The Grayscoh Republic is the second largest sovereignty in Prima. It is the successor state of the Velsyl Empire which collapsed during a civil war and ended when the Velsyl Imperial Family, losing the war, was betrayed and killed by the empire's generals. They reformed the state into a republic where the four territories of the Republic each elect a representative and those 4 representatives unanimously appoint a chancellor who serves as the head of state. The practice of magic is banned is Grayscoh. That, combined with the history of the civil war (initiated by an ancestor of the Velfarr Royal Family), leaves significant tension/animosity between the Republic and the Velfarr Kingdom. There are many in Grayscoh who want to have a broader and friendlier relationship with Velfarr, but also many who want no relationship at all or even wish for war with Velfarr.
There is a small part of what is "officially" Velfarr territory inhabited by people known as the Qaisok in Velfarr. In reality there are four distinct peoples there: the Qaisok, Suna, Kinilat, and Yuocha. But as the current territory was historically just the Qaisok's and they make up most of the population, modern Velfarr inaccurately lumps them all together. The Qaisok are nomadic pastoralists as their land is broadly unfit for agriculture. The Suna, Kinilat, and Yuocha used to be agriculturalist states living in other areas now under Velfarr control. While there is a mutual desire to try and negotiate with Velfarr to return at least some of their former territory to them, they cannot agree on their old borders and each have conflicting claims on the same pieces of land.
There is a city (Whitecap) also de jure in Velfarr, but is de facto under control of two large organized bandit groups. One of which primarily targets Velfarr military and nobility, while the other happily targets those and any other vulnerable individuals/caravans/etc. The two groups dislike each other, but maintain a tense peace (within Whitecap, at least) as a war between them would weaken them to the point that Velfarr would likely attempt to retake the city.
SYNOPSIS
Spoiler
Untold 2 is an homage and love letter to the early Final Fantasy titles (primarily FF, FF2, and FF4). The primary gameplay loop is a top-down exploration of a large world map and varied dungeons rewarding the player with loot, lore, story progression, or any combination of those. Within the dungeons the player's 4 member party will encounter varied groups of enemies that the party fights in a side-view, active time battler (ATB ) system, nothing fancy there. The player's main character is assigned 1 of 8 classes based on early answers they provide to some questions and shortly after they are able to customize the combination of the classes of the other 3 party members, max 2 of any class. This yields 266 mechanically distinct parties available to the player, similar to FF which has 126 distinct party compositions and is what made it so replayable for me.
Untold 2 has the classic JRPG high fantasy genre with its story set in a single world (Prima) within a much larger universe. The player character’s call to adventure is the murder of their father due to reasons quickly discovered to be related to the death of their mother 15 years ago. Resolving to avenge their parents, the player character departs from their humble village in pursuit of the killer. Their revenge quest quickly becomes entangled in a broader crisis with great historical context, culminating in a final confrontation where what must be done to exact vengeance and what must be done to save the world are one and the same.
My goal with Untold 2 was to make a game with a comparable experience to and evocative of the same feeling of playing early FF titles that I fell in love with as a child. I have aimed to emulate what made those games so enjoyable for me and incorporate novel pieces/pillars that I wished had been included in them. The biggest pillar for the game is having a complete and full world within which a story takes place, rather than a world designed around a story. One big piece for this is having the presence of historical context and broader universe/world lore that causally informs the story. The entire history of Prima from its creation to the beginning of the player character’s story is developed (with varying levels of granularity, of course) and can be discovered by the player via cut-scenes, optional dialogue with NPCs, and interactables. The other is making a large and explorable world full of completely optional and sometimes completely story irrelevant locations. The world map is 450x450 tiles and contains more than 40 optional locations comprised of dungeons, settlements, castles, bandit camps, etc. The discovery and exploration of these reward the player with unique equipment, lore, boss fights, miscellaneous loot, or some combo of those.
IMAGES/SCREENSHOTS
Spoiler
A world map of Prima, 450x450 - 1 pixel = 1 tile
Party entering Hohbt, the Economic Capital of Velfarr and the largest city (by population and area) in Prima.
Party approaching Gemranta, Chief Physic, in a destroyed room, within Sirun-shar, the Magic Capital of Velfarr.
Player character, an Elemental, and their father fight bandits in the tutorial battle.
Party (from top to bottom: Magi Duelist (F), Magi Duelist (M), Ranger (M), Monk (F)) engages Yehkon and its cultist follower, whom Yehkon is about to Crush.
CHARACTERS
Spoiler
The Wizard Chiefs are the most prominent NPCs that the player character will interact with repeatedly over the course of the game, revealing history of both the world and the player character's family over time as well as often directing them to their next objective.
Hemen
is the 17th Chief of Magical History. He is 78 years old and a Physic. His position and age have led to him currently being the unofficial, but de facto leader of the Wizard Chiefs.
Kunlan
is the 26th Chief of Magical Items. She is 63 years old and a Magi Duelist. She was a close friend of the player character's mother and is potentially the most powerful wizard in Prima at the beginning of the game.
Maltholos
is the 20th Chief Elemental. He is 48 years old and an Elemental (obviously). He was a young prodigy with great ambition who became the youngest Wizard Chief ever appointed, for a few years, at least.
Gemranta
is the 19th Chief Physic. He is 55 years old and a Physic. Gemranta was only a few years older than the player character's mother, they grew up training together, amicably competing to become the next Chief Physic.
Syntristia
is the 21st Chief Magnyfic. She is 36 years old and a Magnyfic. Syntristia is the youngest wizard to ever be appointed. She founded a merchant guild that is able to use her novel Magnyfic spells to outcompete other merchants and has been forcing many to consolidate together to stay afloat.
PARTY MEMBER CLASSES
Spoiler
Warrior
classes generally rely on their physical talents to be effective in combat, but have learned to harness magic in certain niche ways, and to varying degrees, to enhance and expand their capabilities.
Hospitaller
- It is said that the first Hospitallers were Velsyl imperial knights charged to protect colonies and their inhabitants during the Empire’s expansion onto the Silverful continent. Distinct from other frontline-fighting comrades, Hospitallers are duty-bound to protect the vulnerable and wounded, utilizing all manner of heavy weapons and armor as appropriate. Inspired by the medical prowess on the battlefield of Yuocha Physics they faced, Hospitallers eagerly learned the basics of Physic magic to heal allies and amplify their own attacks early in the Qaisok Wars.
"Hospitallers are physically tough, both offensively and defensively, although we are a bit slow. We use spears, swords, large shields, and heavy armor. Hospitallers also have unique skills which can help protect our allies or inflict Fire, Thunder, and Light damage."
Shinobi
- Shinobi are fleet-footed warriors, trained to strike first and hamstring enemy capabilities before they have a chance to act. Said to have originated in an elusive Qaisok school of Elemental assassins driven underground during the Qaisok Wars, they are trained to use bows to pick off enemies at range and dual-wield daggers to strike swiftly and repeatedly in close combat.
"Shinobi are the fastest out there. We will act before and more often than anyone else. We can fire bows, dual wield daggers, and wear light armor. We can also learn Minor Elemental spells and get access to unique skills which can impair enemies and inflict Thunder, Wind, and Dark damage."
Ranger
- Rangers are descended from eagle-eyed Qaisok hunters who could strike down great beasts with a single devastating shot. These fighters are trained to precisely and ferociously strike foes at critical points with both arrows and whips, supposedly to preserve elemental harmony in nature. Centuries of spiritual kinship with nature lets Rangers imbue their attacks with Wind, Water, and Earth elements and even invoke spirits to fight with them.
"Rangers are resilient and quick. Bows allow us to avoid damage more often, while with whips we can wield small shields for more bulk. We also wear light armor. Rangers also get unique skills that can inflict Wind, Water, and Earth elemental damage to single or multiple targets."
Monk
- Monks are spiritual martial artists who originally learned to fight from observing legendary creatures near their remote monasteries. They excel at applying their unrivaled physical strength in hand-to-hand combat. Cursory meditation on mysterious ancient magic enables them to channel Earth, Water, and Ice elements through their fists.
"Monks are the strongest there are, and we punch our foes with both hands! We can equip light armor and gloves, the tougher they are the harder we can punch! Additionally, monks have unique skills which allow us to inflict Earth, Ice, and Water damage to enemies!"
Wizard
classes generally focus on perfecting specific aspects of the arcane. Utilizing their specialization to maximize their impact in combat. Most only begrudgingly acknowledge that sometimes melee combat is warranted.
Elemental
- These wizards’ ancestry is rumored to originate from a high-ranking member of the Collective, who legend says was the first wizard to ever harness Dark elemental magic into incomparably destructive offensive spells. To this day, Elementals devastate the battlefield at range with a varied arsenal of mastered spells.
"Elementals are offensive wizards, while somewhat flimsy, we deal incomparable damage. We can equip staffs, daggers, and magic armor. We have full access to Minor, Moderate, and Major Elemental spells. These spells can inflict Fire, Thunder, Ice, and Dark damage."
Physic
- Physics are medical experts descended from legendary Yuocha wizards whose magic supposedly granted allies immortality on the battlefield. During the Qaisok Wars, a battle supposedly took place near modern day Celfren, where a Velsyl army of 10,000 was held at bay for weeks by a Yuocha force of just 500, whose wounded in battle one day would reappear the next at full strength, ready to fight again. There, Velsyl learned the true value of Physics.
"Physics are support Wizards who excel at keeping allies alive and healthy. We can equip staffs, whips, and magic armor. Physics are capable of learning Minor, Moderate, and Major Physic spells. These spells restore health, remove status ailments, deal Light damage, and more."
Magi Duelist
- This class of wizards arose from Kinilat mercenaries who wandered alone, seeking knowledge and adventure in all corners of the world. Traveling solo, they necessarily practiced both Elemental and Physic magic, even picking up martial skill in the Velsyl Empire, to protect and care for themselves. Nowadays, Magi Duelists are incredibly flexible fighters, able to fulfill a variety of roles amidst a larger group, as needed.
"Magi Duelists are the jack-of-all trades of classes. We can equip staffs, swords, small shields, large shields, magic armor, and heavy armor. We also can learn both Minor and Moderate Elemental and Physic spells. This allows us to exploit enemy elemental weaknesses and support our allies."
Magnyfic
- Initially studied by the handful of Wizards who first entered Sirun-shar alongside Countess Cornelia, Magnyfic magic helped Count Velfarr’s vastly outnumbered rebel force overpower and topple the Velsyl Empire during Cornelia’s War. Magnyfics developed powerful spells that bolster allies' offense and defense. They protect themselves with magic armor and keep enemies at bay with spears as needed. Their supportive magic helps disadvantaged fighters punch far above their weight against more powerful foes.
"Magnyfics are niche wizards who focus on improving their allies' capabilities. We can equip staffs, spears, and magic armor. Our spells can be used to increase the majority of our allies' stats. As well as provide elemental resistances and other bonuses."
A LITTLE MORE PLOT
Spoiler
The player character and their father return home after a successful job and find a masked/hooded person in their home. They take a necklace that belonged to your mother (who has been dead for ~15 years). This prompts your father to attack the unknown intruder who is revealed to be a wizard as they kill your father with a Fire spell. Knocking the player character out of their way, they coldly warn the hero to not pursue them.
After recruiting other mercenaries who worked with and were friends of your father in Temperanceton to aid you, the hero learns that the Temperanceton Museum has been robbed. An over 300 years old tablet in its collection describing an ancient magical Necklace, crafted by a power-hungry group of wizards long ago, has been stolen. Despite the coincidence, the description of the Necklace's effect is is not particularly interesting. However, upon confronting the thief, the hero learns that the stolen tablet is a fake.
The real tablet is given to them shortly after by Alstur, who claims to be an old friend of your mother. He vaguely warns the hero of some danger potentially developing and directs them Kunlan, the Chief of Magical Items, who has a home to the north in the town of Celfren. Claiming Kunlan can answer their questions properly, he warns the player not to read the tablet as he hasn't, for knowing the contents would permanently endanger them.
Despite Celfren lying quite close to Temperanceton, it will be a long time before the hero manages to find her, traversing an entire continent and then some to do so. Upon finally delivering the tablet to Kunlan, the hero learns the stakes are far higher than imagined, and that vengeance should be the least of their concerns. That said, it may very well be achievable along the way as the hero ingrains themselves in the unveiled crisis... and learns what their mother's role in it was.
AND, IN THE NEAR FUTURE, MUCH MORE TO COME IN FOLLOW-UP POSTS...

posts.body:
AN INTRODUCTION TO THE DEVELOPER AND GENESIS OF UNTOLD
Spoiler
When I was 10 years old I got my first real introduction to video games. My parents gave me a Game Boy SP and a Namco Museum cartridge that contained a number of classic arcade games, including some which were favorites of my father’s when he was younger, such as Ms. Pac-Man and Galaga. While I thoroughly enjoyed playing those (except for Dig Dug), shortly after that gift, we visited one of my uncles (roughly a decade younger than my dad) who, upon learning of my new GBSP, gifted me a cartridge of Final Fantasy 1 & 2 Dawn of Souls, containing remakes of games from his youth.
I had never seen nor played anything like them before and fell absolutely in love with these two games. I did not count, but I am confident that I have played through Final Fantasy 2 over a dozen times and Final Fantasy well over twenty. Naturally, I pursued other FF titles, with Final Fantasy 4 also becoming another favorite of mine. Later FF games moving away from top-down 2D graphics and steadily shifting more and more out of high fantasy settings towards steam-punk/sci-fi ones removed the luster of the franchise’s newer titles for me personally. So as I progressed through my teenage years separate franchises/titles took over my interest.
While I was playing through FF1 and 2 over and over again, the games’ shortcomings (in my eye) became more and more concrete to me. I couldn’t help but refine the absent pieces that could improve these games I already considered favorites. In my senior year of high school, by chance, I encountered the RPG Maker 2003 software, which immediately consumed my attention. I had never thought of making a game like those I adored. I had subconsciously assumed it just wasn’t an option, but suddenly there was a tool in reach that consciously changed that. Without any planning, I dove into the deep end, straight into RPG Maker 2003 haphazardly learning and experimenting with all the capabilities and tools it provided. I now had the ability to create a game in the style of Final Fantasy that I loved, but including all the missing pieces I had contemplated over my many playthroughs (I will cover at least some of these in a separate post). In less than two years I had a
“finished”
game comparable in scale to Final Fantasy. I called it Untold (the genesis of that name will also be explained in its own post).
Untold was
not a good game
(to many Untold 2 won’t be either, but if all you had ever played was the first, two would feel like a masterpiece), even in the context of it being made by a solo developer with no relevant training/experience (aside from having spent hundreds of hours playing JRPGs). Because I eagerly jumped in blind, Untold’s method of development was poor (to put it mildly). While I quickly created a bare-bones, high-level framework of a universe, narrative, and major plot beats, basically everything else was entirely created as I reached it. I finished everything in the current part of the plot prior to putting any real thought into what followed. I designed the map(s), developed the story/characters/dialogue as well as the present items/equipment/services and their prices, implemented the plot progression logic, created relevant encounters and the foes in them, set appropriate music and other sound design pieces, etc. before doing any of that for the next part of the game the player would encounter, and you can tell. This is not a good way to make a game, at least not if you want a decent game (maybe you could make a game structured like Portal that way and have it still turn out pretty okay? Probably still no). That said, I do still take great pride in Untold, not because it is a game that I would ever want to share, but because of what I learned in how to more effectively use this tool and what many of my mistakes/shortcomings more broadly were throughout the game making process.
During my time making the first Untold, I also actively developed the lore of the broader universe the game’s story takes place in, as well as the early pieces of what would become my next project: Untold 2. I was finished with Untold in my 19th summer and was excited to begin working on Untold 2 properly, which I had only allowed to exist as a mix of eclectic thoughts in my head so as to not distract me from completing the first one. That summer I purchased RPG Maker VX Ace, excited to get to work in the newer release of this software with its many clear improvements. This time, I would do it properly. Or, at least as properly as an untrained 18 year old with only one other terrible game’s worth of experience under their belt. Regardless, my plans for the development process of Untold 2 were much more refined (most importantly: just actually having a plan this time).
Unfortunately, unlike its predecessor, Untold 2 would not be completed in under 2 years. In August, after less than two months, I started undergrad. My
time and priorities quickly became consumed
by other things. Classes certainly, however, I would be lying if I said they were my primary time sink. I did not regularly study and actively avoided classes with much graded homework, as I also did not do much of the homework I was assigned (I was a great test taker and
essay writer
, but not a good student). The more “extracurricular” activities available to college students were what pulled most of my attention that could have gone towards Untold 2. It would get consideration every now and then, usually when I had a spur of the moment inspiration that I had to write down and flesh out to have it properly remembered. It was only after I started grad school 4 years later that I decided to commit and set aside my Fridays and Saturdays to work on Untold 2.
Unlike with the first Untold, I knew that I had to plan the entire game, thoroughly, as a
cohesive
whole prior to any implementation work. For over a year I did not even touch RPG Maker software (now RPG Maker MV, then the newest release). I would go to cafes and think, write, read, erase, and write some more (a practice that itself I have fallen in love with and have continued to this day through graduating and now working full-time, I am in a café right now writing this). To date I have filled up over 200 pages across 3 notebooks with my hard-to-read, ADHD handwriting. The story, characters, geography, poorly sketched location layouts (world map, towns, dungeons, etc.), tangential present world lore, historical lore, broader universe lore, enemies and boss fights, party member classes and traits, items and equipment, spells, side-quests, and more, some even quite odd things like long lists of words pulled from a thesaurus to readily have and reference while naming/describing relevant spells, items, and foes, all were planned out over hundreds of hours of scribbling. Many things I still changed even later over time, naturally, but this time I was at least going into the software proper with a complete roadmap.
About a year ago, almost exactly a decade after the completion of Untold, I finally realized, internalized, that Untold 2 was
“close”
to being finished. There were big tasks remaining, but many were beyond my capabilities. Or at least beyond my ability to handle in a way that I would be sufficiently satisfied with to then actually share. I would need outside help. Some of which I have very fortunately already received, which will be covered in another post or two. The rest brings me here, on the search for talent interested and motivated to help me finish this decade long passion project of mine. A project I have spent ~$20,000 on and (given my current hourly rate) invested over $63,000 worth of my time into.
This letter is more of an introduction to the creator of Untold 2 rather than it as a game proper (that should come next). My hope is that I have illustrated not just how much this project means to me, but how much that childhood spent falling in love with these, by my time, overshadowed but foundational JRPG games, meant to me. If one person plays Untold 2 and gets joy from their memories it evokes of playing early Final Fantasy titles when they were younger or if one is inspired afterwards to go play Final Fantasy for the first time, then it will have all been worth it.
I have lost or broken many of my Game Boy cartridges over the years, and my SP has worn with time. The ‘L’ and ‘R’ buttons don’t work consistently nowadays, but luckily those buttons are not important for the Final Fantasy 1 & 2 Dawn of Souls experience. As of last night, my old SP charges, powers on, and (sometimes with a quick breath to clear the dust) those two little games that started it all play just as I remember when I was 10.

posts.author: Untold
posts.body:
A DEEPER INTRODUCTION TO UNTOLD 2
Spoiler
Untold 2 will likely receive a new title prior to it being released to the public. To me, as I worked on it, it was the second game in the Untold universe. As such the working title “Untold 2” made perfect sense to me. However, the first game has never been published, so a title change is likely warranted to mitigate consumers’ confusion (not to mention that Untold 2 is also a prequel to the first Untold game). Then again, it’s
kinda funny
to have the first game labeled “2”, so who knows, not me.
Untold 2 is a standard 2D top-down, sideview battler RPG, as the basics of the RPG Maker software enables. It should feel very familiar to players with experience playing the early Final Fantasy titles. Across those titles there is still a significant amount of differences stylistically and mechanically. One major difference between Final Fantasy and Final Fantasy 4 is the introduction of the Active Time Battle (ATB ) in 4, replacing the basic global turn-based battle system used previously.
ATB was a genuinely monumental development. It directly addressed one of the shortcomings of the first FF, in particular. Which was that there was
no reason to ever use
the Thief/Ninja class, a melee oriented class with eventual access to low-level Black Magic spells. However, if you want a magic user with decent physical attack, the Red Mage/Wizard fully outclasses it, getting access to higher level Black Magic and White Magic. And for physical attacks, the Knight and Monk are superior (with the Monk able to inflict the most physical damage and the Knight having a wider array of weapons and armor it can wield). Given a battle system where everyone gets one action per turn, the Thief/Ninja being “fastest” yields little gameplay advantage over the other aforementioned classes. ATB balances weaker but faster characters by them taking more actions overall per fight. So in Untold 2, the Chevalier (effectively the FF Knight) is offensively and defensively stronger than the Shinobi (effectively the FF Ninja), however, the Shinobi is going to get ~50% more turns in combat. Making it genuinely advantageous depending on the situation and/or preferable depending on what the player likes.
There will be (or is, depending on the date) a post focused on the classes of Untold 2, but I want to briefly discuss the party. This game attempts to blend the heavily variable party system of FF1, which I love (the replay value from being able to pick so many objectively bad/bizarre combinations is great, Monk + White Mage x3 is a favorite of mine), with the much stronger story ingrained and motivated characters of FF2, 4 and most other titles that sacrificed much of that customizability. There is the standard 4 party member set-up in Untold 2. The main character who is personally greatly invested in the story can still be any 1 of the 8 available classes. The three remaining party members can be freely chosen in the early-game by the player out of all 8 classes.
Specifically, there are two heroes (one masc, one fem - mechanically identical) of each class, both of which can be put in the party, if desired. For example, a player’s party could simply consist of two Chevaliers and two Shinobi.
This
yields 266 (mechanically) distinct party combinations. (And if you count the masc vs. fem choice as distinct options that becomes 1,820 party combos, but I do not count that.) For reference, in Final Fantasy there are 126 unique party compositions to choose from. My hope is that players who derive enjoyment from experimenting with party customizability and those who appreciate/care more about their character’s narrative journey can both be satisfied.
Regardless of whatever the party the player chooses, they should be able to successfully progress through the main plot and explore the vast world of Untold 2 with as little or as much
grinding
as they prefer. Exploration is a foundational principle of Untold 2 and Untold as a universe. In many games, including FF titles, the worlds they are set in are clearly built around the story. But this direction of causality is reversed in reality: stories are born by and grown within the world. In Untold 2, my hope is that the player will not feel as though the myriad of locations visited have been made to facilitate their journey, but rather that their journey is formed and molded within the history, geography, and peoples of the world. As such, while the story will move the player throughout most of the world, there are over 40 completely optional locations they can encounter tucked away throughout the entire
world map
. A world map which should feel, intentionally, vast. Balancing overworld travel to evoke the sense that you are, in fact, traveling great distances, without making it feel overly onerous was tricky, and tough to evaluate.
As the player travels from place to place their party will grow stronger, not just from leveling up, but also by
purchasing equipment
and magic tomes that, depending on the class, will improve their capabilities or expand their options in combat. There are three classes of armor (Heavy, Light, Magic), within which exist Head, Body, Shield, and Accessory pieces. In complement to the armor, there are seven classes of weapon (Spear, Sword, Dagger, Whip, Bow, Glove, Staff), two of which each class (excluding Monk) can wield. There are three types of magic: Elemental (spells which inflict damage of a variety of elements),
Physic
(curative spells that restore health, remove status effects, revive fallen party members, and more), and Magnyfic (support spells which buff party members’ stats, remove buffs/debuffs from allies and foes, even add elemental resistances, and more). Elemental and Physic spells are further subdivided into 3 levels: Minor, Moderate, and Major, access to which depends on party member class. Lastly, each of the 4 warrior classes have unique skills, gained over time by level-up, which have a variety of effects, notably including the ability to inflict a variety of elemental damage depending on the skill. The effectiveness of equipped weapons and armor and utilized skills/spells will vary significantly depending on the combat situation (especially for the Magi Duelist). Exploiting inherent enemy weaknesses and resisting their strengths will be crucial, if not for survival, certainly to
speedy progression
.
Speaking of progression speed, in my rough estimation of playtime, if a player were to play through the main story with no exploration and minimal grinding, I expect it to take ~20 hours. If you’ve played through FF2, I expect it would take you a bit less time to get through Untold 2. Like FF, the main plot is linear. While I greatly enjoy player agency, branching plot is exponentially more difficult to implement. Instead, there are two effectively unmarked quests which do have multiple outcomes depending on player choice. While they do not directly impact the main story, they can furnish unique equipment which can aid you in the main story. If you’re a
completionist
, like me, who likes to thoroughly explore and collect everything, play time should roughly double, although that is even trickier for me to estimate.
This high-level overview hopefully gives you a decent idea of what the player experience will be like and how much it
matches up
with your preferences. In summary, Untold 2 should feel familiar to early Final Fantasy titles, but with some clear additions/considerations that would improve, at the very least, my experience as a player. If you enjoy(ed) FF1, 2, and 4, I believe I have crafted a novel experience that you can similarly appreciate.

posts.body:
A BRIEF TANGENT ON HOW-THINGS-GOT-NAMED
Spoiler
There are a lot of NPCs, cities, castles, etc. in Untold 2 that needed names early on as the world was being developed. While the player experiences the game fully in English, in a complete world with thousands of years of history,
multiple languages
would develop. In a humble nod to this, the majority of the custom names were generated through a process of translating certain keywords related to the person/place into a number of different languages and mixing phonetics pulled from those until arriving at a word that just felt right. French and Arabic were the most utilized, but others also contributed including Farsi, Japanese, Spanish, and German. At this point I have forgotten what the source words for most of the custom names are as I did not track that at the time (I now wish I had), but there are some that are more obvious. For example:
Spoiler
k’Argent (built where Velsyl troops first landed on the Silverful continent) is basically just silver in French
The “viento” in Rihvienton (the religious city built in proximity to Enlil, the wind beast) is wind in Spanish
Bergescon is a city built into the side of a mountain and "Berg" is mountain in German
And "sirun", from Sirun-shar (the hidden Magic Capital of the Velfarr Kingdom), is secret in Arabic

posts.body:
THE SETTLEMENTS OF PRIMA
SILVERFUL CONTINENT
Spoiler
Temperanceton:
Tucked between two mountain ranges to the north and south, with oceans to the east and west, this town is arguably one of the most remote in Prima. Despite this, it is the location of the first ever historical museum. A museum which even has an over 300 year old Collective tablet on display.
Celfren:
Lying on the northside of a mountain range from Temperanceton, this city is contemporarily most known for hosting a residence of Kunlan, Velfarr's Chief of Magical Items.
White Cap:
So far north that it is continuously blanketed in snow, this formerly Suna and later Velsyl city is officially part of the Velfarr Kingdom, but is de facto under control of two large and well-organized bandit groups: the Arch Crows, led by Clair and the Blood Bulls, led by Jyakobv.
Oassk:
Standing between two great lakes, this city and its surrounding territory are claimed to have previously belonged to the Suna, Yuocha, and Kinilat by each of their contemporary peoples.
Yasifa:
Town built by worshipers of Esmerelda, in proximity of the Storm Temple, around which Esmerelda is often sighted. Despite lying as far north as White Cap and Fereifrond, the climate in the surrounding area is practically tropical.
k'Argent:
A noble, made obscenely wealthy from their silver mines, funded the Velsyl Empire's first expedition to what would come to be known as the Silverful Continent. This city was established where this expeditionary team first landed. To the noble's dismay, none of the mining operations they attempted around the city were particularly successful.
Faviyesid:
Town built by worshipers of Esmerelda, in proximity of the Rotten Hollow, around which Esmerelda is often sighted.
Densil:
Located  due east of Celfren, this village was razed to the ground by Velfarran forces during their advance across the Silverful Continent towards the end of Cornelia's War.
Flowing Camp:
Not intentionally a permanent settlement. This tent city in Qaisok land constantly has as many nomads stopping in it as those who are leaving, effectively creating a permanent settlement, despite the absence of large scale agriculture. Due to this, the leaders of the Qaisok, Suna, Kinilat, and Yuocha can be often be found here.
VELSYL CONTINENT
Spoiler
Hohbt:
Also known as the Economic Capital of Velfarr. The largest city in Prima and the site of Syntristia's Magnyfic Guild's headquarters.
Fereifrond:
Town built by worshipers of Esmerelda, in proximity of Glacier Valley, around which Esmerelda is often sighted.
Castle Naafbun:
Established by the Velsyl Empire to control a sparsely populated territory, it is now governed by General Ulak of the Velfarr Kingdom, who specializes in training Defense.
Velsyl:
Also known as the Political Capital of Velfarr. Despite now serving as the capital of a state that destroyed the Velsyl Empire, the long established name was too culturally ingrained to disappear.
Castle Hilsa:
Established by the Velsyl Empire to control a sparsely populated territory, it is now governed by General Bronfeld of the Velfarr Kingdom, who specializes in training Spirit.
Rihvienton:
Town originally built by worshipers of Esmerelda, in proximity of the Gale Tower, around which Esmerelda is often sighted.
Castle Sablis:
Established by the Velsyl Empire to control a sparsely populated territory, it is now governed by General Ilyss of the Velfarr Kingdom, who specializes in training Intelligence. After an unorganized retreat to the castle following a Velsyl army's defeat outside of Rihvienton, the Imperial 1st Cavalry was trapped and decimated at Castle Sablis.
Castle Aswah'ahbal:
Established by the Velsyl Empire to control a sparsely populated territory, it is now governed by General Ilyss of the Velfarr Kingdom, who specializes in training Agility.
Bergescon:
Built into the side of a massive mountain, despite being in a southeastern corner of the Velsyl Continent it is the second largest city in the Velfarr Kingdom. A disgraced Grayscoh doctor, Olivier Piedmont, has taken up residence in the city.
Castle Bouvert:
Established by the Velsyl Empire to control a sparsely populated territory, it is now governed by General Lysa of the Velfarr Kingdom, who specializes in training Attack.
Elster:
The only city in the Grayscoh Republic not located on the Helcott continent. After the fall of Bergescon and defeat of the remaining Velsyl imperial army at Castle Bouvert, Elster was quickly put under siege by Velfarr forces, leading to the Empire's surrender.
Falfanor:
An abandoned city a Velfarr citizen named Byron is trying to rebuild. Located in a system of valleys that also hid a Collective outpost, the city was ravaged during the Collective War. Additional stressors and conscription from the following civil war eventually led to the city being fully abandoned as the dwindling number of inhabitants could no longer survive.
HELCOTT CONTINENT
Spoiler
Provenance:
The primary port city of the Grayscoh Republic. The site of the departure of Velsyl's first invasion fleet towards what would become known as the Velsyl continent.
Hibarr:
Town originally built by worshipers of Esmerelda (a practice which is now banned in the Grayscoh Republic), in proximity of the Tidal Grotto, around which Esmerelda is often sighted.
Grayscoh:
The eponymous capital of the Grayscoh Republic. An ancient fortress, the Velsyl Imperial Family traces their origin to the surrounding territory, if not the castle itself. However, the formal establishment of a "Velsyl Empire" did not occur until the foundation of the city of Velsyl during Velsyl expansion onto what would come to be known as the Velsyl Continent.
Sephyir:
The second most populous city on Prima and the most populous of the Grayscoh Republic. Surrounded by impassable mountains to the east, north, west, and with multiple fortresses to the south, it is arguably the most secure city of all Prima.
R'KANIIN ARCHIPELAGO
Spoiler
r'Kaniin:
Town originally built by worshipers of Esmerelda, in proximity of the Volcanic Cavern, around which Esmerelda is often sighted. Control of the city and the rest of the archipelago was given to the Velfarr Kingdom as part of the Velsyl Empire's surrender deal.
??????
Spoiler
Sirun-shar:
Despite desperate attempts by Velsyl imperial scouts during Cornelia's War and many a curious explorer over the following centuries to discover the location of the Magic Capital of Velfarr on Prima, the city's location remains unmarked on world maps.

posts.body:
The following is a quick write-up from a writer I contracted and have been working with for the past 7 months, referred to here just as DJ Jones for now per their request (my own name is also censored, wanting to maintain anonymity for now but will gladly openly share with anyone I personally work with). They generously agreed to share this brief description of their experience working on this project and some of their background:
Spoiler
[The developer] brought me onto [their] team to develop the lore and narrative elements for Untold 2. I’ll briefly say the business and logistical elements of our relationship - contracts, finances, payments, and maintaining consistent communication - have been stellar. Very professional. Next, I’ll discuss my storytelling inspirations and how they fit into [the developer’s] overall vision. It is no secret that Untold 2 is a love story to early JRPGs; specifically the first couple of Final Fantasy games. I first considered games from my childhood like Children of Mana and Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance. But I was especially fascinated by the work of Fromsoftware’s team - namely Elden Ring. I was inspired by how they developed a precursor world - rich with everyday stories and fantastic adventures - and then destroyed that world in a cataclysm. What remained was a new world, and more specifically, the world that player characters would interact with. That symbiosis between destruction and reconstruction was probably the most important idea I used while helping [the developer] develop the world (and consequently, the dialogue) of Untold 2. Collaborating with full-time MIT physicists (and science fiction enthusiasts) helped us further the Untold experience by adding a real-life vocabulary to describe some of the game’s odder narrative elements. Put more simply, we successfully leverage real scientific concepts and verbiage to flesh out a fantastic fictional world. In conclusion I would say my experience writing for [the developer] revolves around those two worlds: Japanese role playing games (old and new) and real-life scientific theory. The result is the world and dialogue of Untold 2, which I am excited to be a part of.
[\SPOILER]
- DJ Jones

If I may make a suggestion: A lot of these are very wordy and really don't give the player any reason to play the game in the end. You really want these to excite people to play the game by telling them about it, and keeping it to the point.
Also I got a question on this:
Untold said:
The rest brings me here, on the search for talent interested and motivated to help me finish this decade long passion project of mine. A project I have spent ~$20,000 on and (given my current hourly rate) invested over $63,000 worth of my time into.
Click to expand...
What was the 20k spent on exactly? Nothing here has shown any evidence that much was spent as all we've seen comes with the engine, which last time I checked costs < $100.

Oh for sure, this is more for recruitment of needed talent rather than marketing.
